parsed_output.paper_title: TRIMMED $k$-MEANS: AN ATTEMPT TO ROBUSTIFY QUANTIZERS
parsed_output.authors_year: J. A. Cuesta-Albertos, A. Gordaliza and C. Matrán, 1997
parsed_output.research_question: How to robustify $k$-means clustering through 'impartial trimming' (self-determined by the data), establish the mathematical existence and strong consistency of trimmed $k$-means, and analyze optimal trimming regions and practical computational performance.
parsed_output.context: Quantization of random variables and $k$-means clustering based on minimizing expected penalty functions suffer from instability and lack of robustness against outliers (e.g., standard joint location M-estimators or unrobust quantizers fail when extreme values are introduced). While trimming is a standard robust technique, traditional trimming suffers from arbitrariness in selecting removal zones. This paper extends Gordaliza's impartial trimming methodology to $k$-means to robustify clustering while avoiding arbitrary zone selection.
methods: Formulation of $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-means using trimming functions $\tau \in \tau_\alpha$ that generalize indicator functions of sets to allow partial participation and avoid arbitrary direction selection.
Mathematical analysis of optimal trimming regions, proving that best trimming functions essentially coincide with indicator functions of unions of $k$ balls of equal radius (Corollary 3.2).
Proof of existence of trimmed $k$-means (Theorem 3.1) and derivation of strong consistency properties via continuity results and the Skorohod representation theorem (Theorem 3.4, Theorem 3.6).

Simulation study using a simulated annealing based algorithm in Matlab on bivariate normal mixtures contaminated by outliers and inlayers to evaluate cluster recovery, anomaly detection, and mean estimation performance.
main_findings: The best trimming function for the $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-mean essentially coincides with the indicator function of a nonpathological set: the union of $k$ balls with the same radius (Corollary 3.2).
Trimmed $k$-means induce a partition of the optimal ball into $k$ clusters where each cluster center is a $\phi$-mean of the corresponding cluster (Proposition 3.3).

Under general conditions including the continuity of the limit probability distribution and uniqueness of the trimmed $k$-mean, empirical trimmed $k$-means are strongly consistent, converging in Hausdorff distance and in variation (Theorem 3.4, Theorem 3.6).

Simulations demonstrate that simulated annealing successfully computes trimmed $k$-means in practice, effectively detecting anomalies and estimating cluster means under high contamination, though low trimming levels can introduce estimator bias due to proximity between clusters.
assumptions: The penalty function $\phi: \mathbb{R}^+\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ is continuous, nondecreasing, with $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(x)\to \infty$ as $x\to \infty$.
The underlying random vector $X$ has a probability distribution $P_X$ that is continuous (or absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure for specific boundary properties).
The true number of clusters $k$ is known and specified in advance.
limitations_explicit: There is an absence of a deterministic optimal (nonexhaustive) algorithm to choose the optimal trimming set.
Every cluster obtained with the method is spherical and all clusters share the same radius, meaning nearby nonspherical or differently shaped clusters may be poorly detected.

The breakdown point of the $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-means depends heavily on the data and can be low if the underlying proportion of anomalous points in a given cluster setup is large relative to $\alpha$.

potential_open_questions.question: How can trimmed $k$-means be extended or modified when clusters have non-spherical shapes or unequal dispersion radii?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The theoretical characterization shows optimal trimming sets and clusters are restricted to unions of balls of equal radius, making it difficult to properly model nonspherical or heterogeneous cluster dispersions.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Section 4, Page 9
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt:
Note that, from Corollary 3.2, it follows that relatively nearby clusters could be badly detected if they are nonspherical or even if their shapes are too different because, according to that corollary, every cluster obtained with our method is spherical and all of them have the same radius. Therefore, the ideal model would be one consisting of spherical, not too close, clusters. Moreover, in that ideal model, the anomalous observations should appear clearly separated from the nonanomalous ones.

Here we have chosen a sample of situations in which each requirement to have an ideal model is violated. Moreover, all of them have in common that many of the anomalous data are not so anomalous because the only restriction we have imposed on them is that they are not allowed to be in the 75% level confidence ellipsoids of the distributions generating the points in the clusters.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: The breakdown point of the $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-mean for a probability distribution supported by $k$ distinct clusters is bounded above by the minimum cluster probability proportion independent of the penalty function.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Examples with uniform distributions on discrete sets containing contamination show that if data naturally contains extraneous points or overlapping structures within the specified number of clusters, trimming cannot prevent contamination from shifting cluster centers arbitrarily if proportion thresholds are breached.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Section 5, Page 16
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt:
A careful look at this example shows that the cause of this behavior of the 2-mean procedure when applied to the uniform probability on A is that, if we are looking for just two clusters, then the set A already contains 1/3 of anomalous points (independently of when those points constitute or do not constitute a new cluster). Therefore, it seems that for probabilities Q, supported by a set which is divided into exactly k clusters with respective probabilities q1, q2, ..., qk, the breakdown point of the $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-mean of Q is, at most, $\inf\{\alpha, q_1, ..., q_k\}$ independently of $\Phi$. Of course, this fact is more apparent when we use other methods like the "two joint medians" example in the Introduction, which is clearly unstable in every circumstance.

In other words, the breakdown point generally depends, of course, on the procedure, but it also depends heavily on the data, in the sense that the same procedure can be highly stable with reasonable clusterized data when considering the right number of clusters, but it can also be very unstable in other cases. This is in some way natural and clearly related to the traditional key problem in cluster analysis: how to choose the number of clusters to look for?

parsed_output.authors_year: Luis Angel García-Escudero, Alfonso Gordaliza, and Carlos Matrán (2003)
parsed_output.research_question: How can trimmed k-means methodology be used as an exploratory graphical tool to distinguish between the bulk of data and outliers, determine the number of clusters (k), and handle different types of contamination?
parsed_output.context: Cluster analysis and outlier detection, specifically building upon trimmed k-means and within-groups variance (k-variance) functionals across various trimming sizes to provide exploratory graphical tools.
methods: Trimmed k-means methodology and empirical trimmed k-variance functionals across varying trimming levels (alpha)
Numerical second derivatives of trimmed k-variance curves to detect abrupt changes or peaks signaling cluster boundaries or excluded groups
An iterative computational algorithm modifying FAST-MCD by replacing the C-step with a 'K-mean-step' based on Euclidean distances
Generalization to mixtures of elliptical distributions using scatter estimation matrices (replacing spherical $W_k$ with covariance determinant criteria)
main_findings: Trimmed $k$-variance curves and their numerical second derivatives provide graphical guidance for choosing the right number of clusters ($k$), identifying cluster sizes, and detecting contamination.
The method distinguishes between different types of outliers, such as outlying groups versus radial outliers, by observing the rate of decrease and peak positions in second derivative curves.
The proposed FAST-MCD inspired algorithm with K-mean-steps offers a feasible computational approach for finding trimmed $k$-means and evaluating variance functionals.
A generalization using covariance-adjusted scatter matrices allows the methodology to succeed on non-spherical (elliptical/linear) cluster mixtures where spherical trimmed k-means fails.
assumptions: Observations follow underlying distributions (often mixtures of spherical or elliptical distributions).

Continuity of distribution functions for theoretical properties like continuity of functionals.

The standard approach is specially aimed at mixtures of spherical distributions, which fails when clusters have arbitrary shapes or different covariance matrices (e.g., highly linear clusters).

candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Spherical trimmed k-means fails on linear or non-spherical clusters because it assumes equal spherical dispersion; incorporating group-specific covariance scatter matrices accounts for arbitrary cluster shapes.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Demonstrated via simulation in Example/Section 4 where standard curves fail on linear clusters, whereas the generalized curve (Eq. 4.1) successfully shows a clear jump at the correct trimming proportion.

parsed_output.paper_title: Implementing the Fisher's Discriminant Ratio in a $k$-Means Clustering Algorithm for Feature Selection and Data Set Trimming
parsed_output.authors_year: Thy-Hou Lin, Huang-Te Li, and Keng-Chang Tsai, 2004
parsed_output.research_question: How can the Fisher's discriminant ratio combined with a $k$-means clustering algorithm be implemented to perform simultaneous feature selection and dataset trimming to improve the statistical significance of 3D-QSAR regression models?
parsed_output.context: In 3D-QSAR modeling (such as CoMFA and PLS), selecting informative variables and eliminating background noise increases the signal-to-noise ratio. While traditional methods focus on selecting field variables, this paper introduces a concomitant feature selection and dataset trimming approach by rejecting inhibitors that fail class separability criteria defined by selected topological descriptors using $k$-means clustering.
methods: Computing 43 molecular descriptors (topological, geometric, electronic, and 3D-QSAR features) for 221 HIV-1 protease inhibitors scaled between 1 and 0.
Dividing inhibitors into classes (primarily five classes) based on $pC_i$ values.
Ranking features using Fisher's discriminant ratio ($C$) and cross-correlation coefficients to select the most class-sensitive descriptors.

Employing a $k$-means clustering algorithm ($k_{mm} = 2$ or $3$) within each class for each selected descriptor to identify a 'bad' cluster with smaller descriptor values containing potential outliers.
Trimming dataset by discarding inhibitors identified in all bad clusters across all selected descriptors.

Evaluating feature selection and regression performance using stepwise variable selection (MREG), linear regression normal equations, cross-validated $q^2$, external validation metrics (Golbraikh and Tropsha), representation entropy ($H_R$), and SYBYL CoMFA PLS / Cerius2 PLS analyses.
main_findings: Concomitant feature selection and dataset trimming using Fisher's discriminant ratio and $k$-means clustering successfully reduced descriptor and inhibitor counts while improving regression statistics.

Selecting the three best topological descriptors ($Z_4, Z_6, Z_3$) retained 98 out of 221 inhibitors (44%) and substantially increased the $q^2$ of SYBYL CoMFA PLS and Cerius2 PLS analyses compared to using the original full dataset.
Scaling descriptor values prior to feature selection is necessary, as unscaled descriptors yielded suboptimal QSAR/conventional features with low information content.
The $k$-means clustering and trimming method performs well when the dataset contains simple decision boundaries between classes.
assumptions: Molecular descriptor values can be appropriately scaled to lie between 1 and 0 to prevent larger dynamic ranges from disproportionately influencing cost functions.

Inhibitors falling into the 'bad' cluster with smaller descriptor values across all selected class-sensitive descriptors represent outliers or low class-sensitivity compounds that should be discarded.
Class separability based on $pC_i$ activity classes correlates with structural descriptors, specifically topological indices.
limitations_explicit: The proposed algorithm is not invariant under a transformation of the variables.

More complicated classification rules (such as Bayesian classifiers) require prior knowledge about the distribution of classes, and alternative separability measures like one-dimensional divergence were less effective than the Fisher's discriminant ratio.

potential_open_questions.question: How can clustering-based dataset trimming be generalized to datasets with complex, non-linear decision boundaries between classes where simple $k$-means bad-cluster identification may fail?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The authors note a weakness of their algorithm is its lack of invariance under variable transformation and state that their success relies on the simplicity of the dataset without complex decision boundaries.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The algorithm's sensitivity to variable transformations and limitations with complex decision boundaries are discussed in the concluding remarks.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: We have randomly altered the order of input for all the 43 descriptors and found that the feature selection result is unchanged. The correlation parameter R2 has also been varied during the feature selection process to examine if there is any significant correlation between the descriptors. No difference in the feature selection result for R2 being set as 1 or 0 is found, suggesting that no severe correlation is present in the set of descriptors computed. We have also applied the feature selection algorithm to the 43 unscaled descriptors and found that the best six descriptors selected are 32 (42.50,3.08), 38 (19.13,3.01), 35 (7.23,3.57), 36 (4.50,0.00), 8 (2.42,3.56), and 17 (1.87,4.81), where the corresponding feature values and information contents are parenthesized first and next, respectively. Although the descriptors identified are four QSAR, one conventional and one MOPAC ones, some of their corresponding information contents are low. This justifies the need for scaling all the descriptor values before performing the feature selection on them. On the other hand, the weakness of our algorithm is also revealed since it is not invariant under a transformation of the variables. Fortunately, the data set we dealt with is simple, and no complex decision boundaries38 are present between classes.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Alternative classification techniques combined with feature selection could provide effective dataset trimming comparable to or exceeding $k$-means clustering without requiring rigid cluster number specifications.
candidate_hypotheses.why_unresolved: The paper notes that other classification techniques might be effective but highlights that more complicated rules like Bayesian classification require prior knowledge of class distributions.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The authors suggest exploring other classification techniques for trimming while noting the trade-offs of more complex rules.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: Instead of focusing on the selection of field variables, we aim at the trimming of the data set by rejecting inhibitors that are unable to match the class separability criteria established for them using some descriptors selected. A random deletion of some inhibitors from the original set would not improve the value of q2 significantly. The descriptors selected are those bearing good class sensitivity. It is interested to find that most of these descriptors are the topological ones. While the k-means clustering scheme performs well in combination with the feature selection process, other classification techniques may be also effective in providing the trimming in the process. However, a more complicated classification rule such as the Bayesian one requires some a priori knowledge about the distribution of classes. All CoMFA experience suggests that the only action capable of changing the sign of a q2 value is realigning some or all of the molecules. Our method will be useful when all the biological data are sound and there are either no structurally obvious ways to align the molecules or those ways fail to produce a satisfactory q2.

parsed_output.authors_year: Alexandros Georgogiannis, 2016
parsed_output.research_question: What are the robustness and consistency properties of robust k-means (RKM), a variant of classical quadratic k-means that borrows ideas from outlier detection in regression via penalized regularization/Moreau envelopes?
parsed_output.context: Over recent years, variations of quadratic k-means have been proposed to robustify performance against outliers through penalized regularization methods or trimming functions. This paper theoretically analyzes the robustness and consistency of robust k-means (RKM), examining its finite-sample breakdown point, performance on well-structured datasets, and relation to trimmed k-means.
methods: Theoretical analysis using variational analysis tools (Moreau envelope, proximal maps, subgradients)
Finite sample breakdown point analysis (universal breakdown point for biased and unbiased proximal maps)
Analysis of restricted robustness on well-structured ((rho_1, rho_2)-balanced) datasets
Consistency analysis using Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) theory and empirical process theory
Synthetic data experiments comparing robust k-means and trimmed k-means on mixtures of Gaussians with varying contamination levels
main_findings: Two outliers are enough to break down the RKM clustering procedure when using biased proximal maps (convex penalties), yielding a breakdown point of 1/n.
RKM with unbiased proximal maps (non-convex penalties) has a universal breakdown point of 2/n for arbitrary datasets.

Despite poor worst-case universal breakdown points, if attention is restricted to well-structured datasets where inlier balls are sufficiently far apart, RKM ignores the influence of outliers when grouping inliers.
RKM exhibits consistency (loss and parameter convergence in probability) with non-asymptotic rates of order O(sqrt(log n / n)) even when penalties are non-convex.
RKM and trimmed k-means (TKM) perform remarkably similarly in practice across accuracy, center estimation error, and outlier detection rates.
assumptions: Observations $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^p$ come from a fixed but unknown probability measure $\mu$ (for consistency) or form a finite set $\mathcal{X}^n$ (for breakdown analysis).
Penalty functions $f_\lambda$ are symmetric, lower semi-continuous (lsc), proper, and bounded from below.
Well-structured datasets possess a (\rho_1, \rho_2)-balanced inlier subset composed of disjoint balls of bounded radius $r$ with centers separated by at least distance $v$.
limitations_explicit: Universal breakdown point analysis shows that RKM can break down with very few outliers (one outlier for convex penalties, two outliers for non-convex unbiased penalties) under arbitrary dataset contamination.
The robust behavior guaranteed by theoretical bounds requires strict structural assumptions on the dataset (well-clustered data with balls far apart).

potential_open_questions.question: Can the universal breakdown point of robust k-means be improved beyond O(1/n) without relying heavily on restricted domain or well-clustered dataset assumptions?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The tight notion of universal breakdown allows arbitrary contamination, causing both RKM and trimmed k-means to break down at very low contamination thresholds, which highlights a mismatch between worst-case theoretical vulnerability and practical robustness.

parsed_output.paper_title: K-means-sharp: modified centroid update for outlier-robust k-means clustering
parsed_output.authors_year: Peter O. Olukanmi and Bhekisipho Twala, 2017
parsed_output.research_question: How can the classical k-means clustering algorithm be modified to be robust to outliers while preserving its structure, simplicity, and efficiency without requiring user intervention or prior knowledge of the number of outliers?
parsed_output.context: Real-world datasets commonly contain noise and outliers, which skew classical k-means clustering because it is a least-squares method. Traditional outlier detection methods often operate in separate pre-processing or post-processing modules, rely on user-supplied parameters, or increase computational cost. This paper proposes a simultaneous clustering and automated outlier detection approach named k-means-sharp (k-means#) that modifies only the centroid update step.
methods: Formulation of k-means-sharp (k-means#) which integrates automatic outlier detection and avoidance into the centroid update step.
Computation of a global point-to-centroid distance threshold T based on the median absolute deviation (MAD) of point-to-centroid distances (using 3 standard deviations, where sigma = 1.4826 * MAD_e).
Exclusion of data points whose point-to-centroid distance exceeds T from the new centroid mean calculation in each iteration.

Experimental evaluation across 10 datasets (2 standard datasets: Iris and Ruspini, plus 4 outlier-contaminated versions of each with gross errors ranging from 5% to 20%) comparing clustering mean squared error and outlier detection performance (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score) against classical k-means over 100 runs per dataset.
Utilization of a 'best so far' stopping/selection strategy over 50 iterations to handle the non-monotonically decreasing cost function caused by the changing inlier set.
main_findings: Given identical initializations, k-means# yields lower mean squared error than classical k-means across all 10 datasets tested.
K-means# achieves an overall average outlier detection accuracy of 90.4% and precision of 86.8%, with moderate recall (52.4%) and F1-score (61.1%).
The algorithm requires neither user intervention nor prior knowledge of the number of outliers and preserves the structural simplicity and efficiency of classical k-means.
assumptions: K-means, being an instance of the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), assumes a Gaussian data distribution, implying that 99.73% of inliers have point-to-centroid distances within 3 standard deviations from the mean.
The population standard deviation can be robustly estimated as sigma = 1.4826 * MAD_e.
A single global threshold T applies adequately across all clusters.
limitations_explicit: The algorithm occasionally encounters rare cases (due to bad random initializations, such as when all initial centroids are outliers) where zero true positives are returned, resulting in undefined precision and F1 scores.

The current implementation uses a single global threshold and a fixed boundary of 3 standard deviations, which may limit performance optimization compared to cluster-specific thresholds or sensitivity tuning.

potential_open_questions.question: How does varying the number of standard deviations for determining the inlier-outlier distinction threshold affect the trade-offs among the various performance metrics?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The choice of 3 standard deviations is fixed in the current study, and the paper notes that altering this boundary is expected to introduce trade-offs in algorithm performance that require systematic investigation.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Future work will involve investigating algorithm sensitivity to the number of standard deviations used for the threshold.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt:
The results summarize the performance improvements achieved due to our proposed modification. Unlike existing threshold-based approaches (see Section III), our threshold need not be supplied by the user. It is computed online using a statistically sound rule (See Section IV). It is expected that our choice of 3 standard deviations as the boundary for inlier point-to-centroid distance, plays a role in the performance of the algorithm. We expect trade-offs among the various performance metrics as this value is varied. In summary, in its ability to detect outliers, the k-means# implementation presented in this paper is highly accurate (90.4% average), highly precise (86.8% average) and moderately sensitive (52.4% average recall).

VI. CONCLUSION
This paper addressed k-means’ sensitivity to outliers while maintaining the algorithm’s basic structure, to preserve simplicity and efficiency. Specifically, we presented a new clustering algorithm named k-means# (pronounced k-means sharp), which modifies only the centroid update step in the original algorithm. In each iteration, putative outliers are detected automatically and excluded from the computation of new centroids. The new cost function is a generalization of the standard k-means’, for which the latter represents a special case in which all points are considered inliers. The new algorithm preserves the ease of implementation for which the classical k-means is known.

We evaluated the impact of this simple modification on the original algorithm. In all cases tested, given identical initializations, k-means# yields better error than k-means. Furthermore, on the overall, its outlier detection mechanism exhibits high (90.4% average) accuracy, high (86.8% average) precision, with moderate recall and F1 score (52.4% and 61.1% averages), in contrast to classical k-means is unable to detect outliers. The algorithm achieves maximum values of 99.2%, 100%, 90% and 92.9%, respectively, of the aforementioned metrics.

A worthwhile direction for future work will be to investigate the sensitivity of the algorithm (in terms of each performance metric discussed) to the choice of the number of standard deviations for determining the inlier-outlier distinction threshold.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: The use of cluster-specific thresholds instead of a single global threshold will improve outlier detection and clustering performance in k-means#.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Different clusters may exhibit varying internal distributions and spread, meaning a single global threshold might miss cluster-specific anomalies that cluster-local thresholds could accurately capture.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Cluster-specific thresholds may improve performance, though they increase computational cost.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt:
A worthwhile direction for future work will be to investigate the sensitivity of the algorithm (in terms of each performance metric discussed) to the choice of the number of standard deviations for determining the inlier-outlier distinction threshold. Furthermore, the use of cluster-specific thresholds in contrast to a single global threshold, may improve performance, and is therefore worth exploring, although this will introduce some increase in computational cost. Lastly, since k-means# preserves the original k-means structure, it can easily benefit from many existing k-means improvements designed to address other drawbacks. Incorporation of some of these should yield increased robustness.

REFERENCES

parsed_output.authors_year: Agrawal, Inamdar, Saurabh, and Xue (2023)
parsed_output.research_question: Can we design a general approximation-preserving FPT reduction from clustering with outliers problems (such as k-MedianOut and k-MeansOut) to their outlier-free counterparts, and thereby obtain optimal FPT approximation algorithms for these problems?
parsed_output.context: Clustering problems with outliers aim to exclude m points from a dataset X and partition the remaining points into k clusters to minimize a cost function. Real-world data are often contaminated with noise, making outlier-robust clustering fundamental. While prior works established polynomial-time approximations or FPT approximations with suboptimal ratios, this paper investigates whether a reduction to the outlier-free case can yield optimal approximation ratios in FPT time parameterized by k and m.
methods: Formulating an outlier-free (k + m)-Median (or (k + m, z)-Clustering) instance by co-locating a facility with each client, yielding a lower bound on the optimal outlier clustering cost.
Computing a polynomial-time τ-approximation for the (k + m)-median instance to establish average radius bounds and partition clients into concentric rings around cluster centers.
Constructing a weighted coreset via uniform sampling within each ring, coupled with a concentration bound (Lemma 1) preserving connection costs even after dropping m outliers.
Enumerating all subsets T of the coreset of size up to m and solving the resulting weighted outlier-free k-median instances using a β-approximation black-box algorithm.
main_findings: A general approximation-preserving reduction from k-MedianOut to k-Median that runs in time ((k + m)/ϵ)^{O(m)} · T(n, k) · n^{O(1)}, producing a (β + ϵ)-approximation given a β-approximation for k-Median.
An optimal (1 + 2/e + ϵ)-approximation for k-MedianOut and a (1 + 8/e + ϵ)-approximation for k-MeansOut in general metrics.
FPT (1 + ϵ)-approximations for k-MedianOut and k-MeansOut in special metrics such as constant doubling dimensions, bounded treewidth graphs, and minor-free graph classes.
Successful extensions of the framework to constrained and generalized variants, including Matroid Median with Outliers, Colorful k-Median, and (k, z)-Clustering with Outliers.
assumptions: The underlying distance function satisfies symmetry and the triangle inequality (for metric clustering).
There exists a β-approximation algorithm for the standard outlier-free k-Median (or k-Median-type) problem with running time T(n, k).
There exists a polynomial-time τ-approximation algorithm for the (k + m)-Median (or outlier-free) problem where τ = O(1).

potential_open_questions.question: Can the FPT running time dependence on the number of outliers m be improved while maintaining tight approximation ratios, or is it possible to achieve approximation guarantees for k-MedianOut matching k-Median with a running time FPT in k and ϵ alone?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The current framework relies on enumerating subsets of size up to m from the coreset, leading to an exponential dependence on m (specifically ((k + m)/ϵ)^{O(m)}). Whether this dependence on m is inherent or can be removed remains open.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Section 5, Page 16
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt:
In this paper, we give a reduction from k-MEDIANOUT to k-MEDIAN that runs in time FPT in k, m, and ϵ, and preserves the approximation ratio up to an additive ϵ factor. As a consequence, we obtain improved FPT approximations for k-MEDIANOUT in general as well as special kinds of metrics, and these approximation guarantees are known to be tight in general. Furthermore, our technique is versatile in that it also gives improved approximations for related clustering problems, such as k-MEANSOUT, MATROID MEDIAN WITH OUTLIERS, and COLORFUL k-MEDIAN, among others.
The most natural direction is to improve the FPT running time while obtaining the tight approximation ratios. More fundamentally, perhaps, is the question whether we need an FPT dependence on the number of outliers, m; or whether it is possible to obtain approximation guarantees for k-MEDIANOUT matching that for k-MEDIAN, with a running time that is FPT in k and ϵ alone.

candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Treating outliers in an optimal solution as virtual centers relates k-MedianOut to (k + m)-Median. By structuring points into concentric rings and applying multiplicative sampling concentration bounds, a coreset of size polynomial in k, m, and log n can preserve clustering costs for all center sets and outlier selections simultaneously.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Section 1.2 and Section 3, Pages 3-4 and 6
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: Our reduction is inspired from the following seemingly simple observation that relates k-MEDIANOUT and k-MEDIAN. Let I be an instance of k-MEDIANOUT, where we want to find a set C of k centers, such that the sum of distances of all except at most m points to the nearest center in C is minimized. By treating the outliers in an optimal solution for I as virtual centers, one obtains a solution for (k + m)-MEDIAN without outliers whose cost is at most the optimal cost of I. In other words, the optimal cost of an appropriately defined instance Ie of (k + m)-MEDIAN is a lower bound on the optimal cost of I. Since k-MEDIAN is a well-studied problem, at this point, one would hope that it is sufficient to restrict the attention to Ie. That is, if we obtain a solution (i.e., a set of k + m centers) for Ie, can then be modified to obtain a solution (i.e., a set of k centers and m outliers) for I. However, it is unclear whether one can do such a modification without blowing up the cost for I. Nevertheless, this connection between Ie and I turns out to be useful, but we need several new ideas to exploit it.

parsed_output.paper_title: Nonparametric framework for the definition, adaptive detection and probabilistic interpretation of outliers
parsed_output.authors_year: Iannaccio & Vichi, 2026
parsed_output.research_question: How can outlier detection be formulated using a universal, domain-agnostic, nonparametric framework with a probabilistic interpretation linked to a false-alarm rate alpha, and how can this framework be integrated into K-means clustering for adaptive trimming (ODK-means)?
parsed_output.context: Outlier detection is a fundamental challenge in data processing, but existing proposals rarely offer a universal, domain-agnostic definition and often rely on heuristic trimming quotas lacking a statistical interpretation. In clustering frameworks like trimmed K-means, a pre-specified proportion of points is iteratively trimmed based on distance to centroids.
methods: Formulation of a Mahalanobis pseudo-isolation outlier score based on k-nearest neighbors starting from a rank h >= 1.
Candidate Cantelli-based outlier thresholds evaluated using running sample means and standard deviations of sorted pseudo-isolations to control false-alarm rate alpha.
Geometric classification of outliers into internal, external, and cluster-specific outliers based on convex hulls.
Integration of the probabilistic outlier detection module into K-means to form the Outlier Detection K-means (ODK-means) algorithm, using weighted K-means with hard or soft trimming.
main_findings: The proposed nonparametric framework establishes a probabilistic definition of anomalies tied to a false-alarm rate alpha and provides a rigorous geometric classification of external, internal, and cluster-specific outliers.

Theoretical analysis reveals three topological properties of the pseudo-isolation score distribution: quiescence (a non-significant outlierness interval), class equivalence (intervals of stable outlier counts), and coalescence (outliers move in groups rather than separating individually).
ODK-means successfully integrates adaptive trimming into K-means, maintaining linear scalability per iteration while avoiding the need to pre-specify a trimming proportion p-hat.

Simulations and methodological tutorials demonstrate that ODK-means outperforms traditional trimmed K-means and Local Outlier Factor (LOF) across various contamination rates and data dispersions, and naturally reduces to standard K-means when no outliers are present.
assumptions: Pseudo-isolation scores have finite mean mu and variance sigma^2 > 0.
Standard asymptotic k-NN theory applies, setting l such that l -> infinity and l/N -> 0 as N -> infinity, with lower rank h set to a small fraction of l.
limitations_explicit: ODK-means inherits all limitations of standard K-means except those related to the presence of outliers (e.g., performance on non-spherical clusters).
The proposal has been developed from a purely methodological perspective, meaning the full range of applicability of its theoretical properties may be partially immediate.

potential_open_questions.question: How can a fully parametric extension of the nonparametric pseudo-isolation framework be developed to derive a closed-form distribution for the pseudo-isolation score and enable exact hypothesis testing?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The current framework relies on nonparametric bounds (such as the Cantelli inequality) because the exact distribution of pseudo-isolations is not derived in closed form, limiting formal exact hypothesis testing for individual outliers.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Future research direction on parametric extension
potential_open_questions.evidence_expert:
Since our proposal has been developed from a purely methodological perspective, the full range of applicability of its theoretical properties may be partially immediate. While advantages like dynamic outlier selection or a clear false-alarm interpretation are easy to appreciate, the related inferential insights offer practical value in applied settings. For instance, in lab environments or controlled baseline trials, researchers often face ambiguous boundary observations. Rather than relying on rigid, arbitrary cutoffs, evaluating the exact false-alarm rate α^⋆ required to flag those specific subjects allows scientists to assess the exact risk/tolerance needed to consider them anomalous. To give another example, when domain experts work with confirmed historical outliers, the evaluation of their α^⋆ provides a theoretically grounded benchmark to calibrate false-alarm budgets for future studies.
We conclude this work by pointing to the main direction for future research: developing a fully parametric extension of this framework to derive a closed-form distribution for the pseudo-isolation score. Achieving an analytical expression for this distribution will enable formal, exact hypothesis testing for individual outliers, providing an even stronger inferential foundation for anomaly detection.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Integrating the nonparametric probabilistic outlier detection engine into alternative clustering frameworks with more flexible cluster geometries (such as Gaussian Mixture Models or subspace clustering techniques) will maintain robust adaptive trimming and outlier categorization performance on complex data structures.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: The outlier detection module is modular and objective-based, meaning its logic can extend beyond spherical K-means to handle non-spherical, overlapping clusters or high-dimensional subspace structures.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Discussion on extending the framework to GMMs and subspace clustering
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: It is worth emphasizing that the proposed framework is not limited to the simple settings shown in the methodological tutorial. Its modular logic extends naturally to more complex geometries and high-dimensional settings. For example, non-spherical or overlapping clusters can be handled by incorporating our detection mechanism into Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs), as discussed in Remark 4. To address the curse of dimensionality, the same logic can be applied to subspace clustering techniques, such as Reduced K-means [21] or Factorial K-means [22]. Finally, the core isolation score itself can be tailored to handle specific structural constraints, such as multi-way data arrays or disjoint component constraints, as treated by XT3Clus [23]. Choosing K-means as our baseline clustering algorithm provided a clear and intuitive foundation, allowing us to showcase the visual mechanics of the proposed framework with minimal complexity. Furthermore, this choice ensures a direct and fair comparison against the most established outlier detection procedures in the literature.

parsed_output.paper_title: Adaptive Federated Baseline K-Means for Lightweight IoT Intrusion Detection: Auto-Thresholding and Robust Statistics Aggregation
parsed_output.authors_year: Mohammed Al Saleh and Joseph Azar, 2026
parsed_output.research_question: How to repair the federated Baseline K-Means mechanism to eliminate merge-induced precision decay, remove manual percentile threshold searches, and control false-positive rates while preserving the statistics-only, semi-supervised communication model suitable for resource-constrained IoT devices?
parsed_output.context: IoT intrusion detection systems require lightweight models that protect data privacy through federated learning while functioning under semi-supervised novelty detection due to scarce attack labels. A cross-layer federated detector called Baseline K-Means (BKM) periodically merges worker statistics via a coordinator to raise recall, but exhibits a systematic side effect: after every merge, precision decays and the false-positive rate climbs because the coordinator recomputes its decision threshold from streaming distances filtered by the closest observed anomaly, progressively tightening and flagging benign traffic. Furthermore, this threshold percentile was hand-tuned.
methods: AF-BKM (Adaptive Federated Baseline K-Means) framework combining two label-free, statistics-only enhancements (E1 and E2).

E1 (Adaptive Auto-Thresholding): Replaces manual percentiles by reading the decision threshold directly from the shape of the benign Mahalanobis-distance distribution using a robust median-absolute-deviation (MAD) rule or a target-FPR calibration.

E2 (Robust, Benignly Anchored Aggregation): Replaces nearest-anomaly threshold tightening with a count/quality-weighted worker mean blended with a trusted benign anchor under a damping factor beta, and recalibrates the global threshold on that trusted anchor.
Trust gate at the coordinator to identify and discard outlier worker threshold candidates scaled by MAD from the median of candidates.

Empirical evaluation using three public datasets (NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, and N-BaIoT) under a non-IID federated protocol with baseline-only MinMax scaling and a disclosed label-blind, full-corpus near-constant filter, across 10 seeds for central ablations and significance testing, alongside sweeps, stress tests (faulty workers, anchor contamination, white-box evasion), and resource profiling.
main_findings: AF-BKM successfully removes the merge-induced precision decay, with first-to-last-epoch precision change improving from -0.134 to -0.002 on NSL-KDD, -0.121 to -0.014 on UNSW-NB15, and -0.170 to -0.009 on N-BaIoT.
Reduces mean false-positive rate (FPR) by 30-64% depending on the dataset, with improvements statistically significant across 10 seeds (Wilcoxon p = 0.002, large effect sizes).
Preserves recall on NSL-KDD and N-BaIoT, while exposing an explicit precision-recall trade-off through a benign target-FPR knob on the harder UNSW-NB15 dataset.

Worker-side model serializes to 5.5-52 KB in closed-form fp32, classifies a packet in 11-27 microseconds on a desktop CPU, and uploads a compact d+3-value summary (160-472 bytes) per merge round, saving 94.6-98.3% compared to sharing covariance matrices.

Robustness and stress evaluations show that fabricated threshold candidates have no direct path to the global threshold because it is anchored, although a fabricated mean reaches it indirectly through the blended centroid, and the anchor-referenced false-positive level remains stable under percent-level anchor contamination.
assumptions: AF-BKM assumes a small, trusted, benign anchor for benign-only calibration and does not use attack labels for thresholding or worker-quality weighting.
The coordinator securely stores the trusted benign anchor, and operational traffic cannot modify the anchor after commissioning.
The inverse covariance matrix is estimated once at the coordinator from the trusted benign anchor and is never re-estimated from worker data.
limitations_explicit: Anchor trust: the false-positive level is held constant with respect to the trusted benign anchor, making the property anchor-relative rather than local when a worker's benign distribution drifts far from it, and under the MAD default it represents a stable level rather than an operator-chosen one.

The non-IID setting modeled in the paper focuses primarily on label skew with a small viability floor, leaving feature-space skew, per-device behavioral drift, and changing traffic mixtures largely unaddressed.
No new physical edge deployment or measured hardware energy consumption was performed; reported resource profiles rely on desktop benchmarks and closed-form fp32 serialization sizes.
All three corpora are recorded datasets rather than evaluations on a live operational network with an active deployment pilot.
Under commissioning-anchor contamination, recall drops sharply once contamination exceeds 2-5% because the underlying sample mean and covariance are non-robust estimators.
The robustness study covers only selected scripted faulty-worker updates, anchor contamination, and white-box evasion, establishing no worst-case guarantee against adaptive adversaries.

potential_open_questions.question: How can streaming concept drift, lightweight drift detectors, or adaptive anchor refresh policies be integrated into AF-BKM so that benign calibration remains valid over extended operating periods?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The current AF-BKM protocol relies on a fixed, one-time trusted benign anchor established during commissioning and does not incorporate streaming drift adaptation mechanisms.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Discussion on future work regarding streaming concept drift and adaptive anchor refresh policies.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: The most immediate extension is streaming concept drift, using lightweight drift detectors or adaptive anchor refresh policies so that benign calibration remains valid over time [21]. The anchor-contamination results argue separately for robust estimation underneath the robust threshold: replacing the sample mean and covariance with a minimum-covariance-determinant estimator [36] would harden the calibration against dirty commissioning windows, since shrinkage [37] improves conditioning but does not, by itself, confer outlier robustness and diagonal, block-diagonal or low-rank covariance summaries could additionally cut communication. A physical deployment pass also remains to be done: on-device timing, memory and measured (rather than estimated) energy on microcontroller hardware, ideally together with a live pilot. Evaluation on further device-centric corpora such as Bot-IoT is a separate open item. Over a longer horizon, AF-BKM could be combined with the earlier ensemble idea, providing a stable, calibrated first-stage BKM signal while lightweight local detectors are invoked only near ambiguous decision regions, which the evasion analysis suggests is where they are most needed.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Replacing the sample mean and covariance estimators with a robust estimator such as the minimum-covariance-determinant (MCD) estimator will harden the global threshold calibration against dirty commissioning windows contaminated by attack traffic.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Anchor-contamination stress tests demonstrate that while the MAD threshold rule survives contamination, the non-robust sample mean and covariance inflate along attack directions, degrading recall.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Discussion on robust estimation underneath the robust threshold to harden calibration against dirty commissioning windows.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: The remaining attack surface identified in the threat model is the commissioning window itself: if attack traffic is already flowing while the anchor is collected, Xa is contaminated before the protocol starts. We measure this directly by replacing a fraction (p ∈ {0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20}%) of the 2000-packet baseline with attack rows before fitting; the contamination then propagates through the scaler, the mean and covariance, the threshold, and the coordinator anchor, as a dirty collection window would. Table 11 and Figure 10 report the measured pattern (NSL-KDD and UNSW-NB15, five seeds). The false-positive rate stays controlled at every contamination level (0.08–0.16 on NSL-KDD, 0.07–0.08 on UNSW-NB15). Recall behaves differently per dataset: on NSL-KDD, it stays within a point of the clean run through p = 2% (0.925 → 0.913, with precision moving from 0.79 to 0.84), whereas on UNSW-NB15, where recall is threshold-sensitive to begin with, it already declines over the same range (0.366 at p = 0 to 0.287 at p = 2%, with substantial seed-to-seed variation). From p = 5% recall drops sharply on both datasets (NSL-KDD, 0.45 at 5% and 0.25 at 10%; UNSW-NB15, 0.18 and 0.13). The MAD threshold is a robust statistic and holds the false-positive level, but the mean and covariance underneath it are not robust estimators, and the planted attack rows inflate the covariance along attack directions, which shrinks attack distances and costs recall. The threshold rule survives contamination; the Gaussian model is the weak point, which argues for MCD or another robust covariance estimator as a hardening step. The tolerated regime therefore rests on an operational assumption rather than a guarantee: commissioning is expected to be a short, supervised phase, and contamination beyond a few percent of that window falls outside what the current estimators absorb.

parsed_output.historical_analysis: The corpus spans nearly six decades of research on partitioning algorithms, starting with MacQueen's foundational introduction of the K-means procedure and its asymptotic properties (P001). Early implementations struggled with sensitivity to anomalous data and initialization. To address this, Cuesta-Albertos et al. formalized 'trimmed k-means' through impartial trimming and optimal spherical balls (P002), which was later expanded into exploratory graphical tools and variance curve analyses by García-Escudero et al. (P003). Over the years, outlier-robust adaptations evolved along several parallel tracks: heuristic-based centroid updates using distance thresholds (P006, P007, P010, P011), regression-inspired robust regularization (P005), convex relaxation frameworks on simplices (P009), rigorous algorithmic approximations with polynomial running time guarantees (P008, P013), and unification frameworks transforming complex problems into generalized K-means (P014). Most recently, research has advanced into nonparametric probabilistic outlier detection frameworks (P015), multi-target classification integrations (P016), and adaptive federated architectures for edge IoT (P017). Across this evolution, a persistent tension remains between theoretical breakdown guarantees under adversarial contamination and practical runtime efficiency on complex, non-spherical datasets.

research_gaps.gap: Lack of deterministic, non-exhaustive algorithms for identifying optimal trimming regions without enforcing strict spherical symmetry and equal dispersion radii across clusters.
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Real-world datasets frequently contain clusters with varying densities, arbitrary non-spherical shapes, or heterogeneous dispersions. Assuming equal-radius spherical optimal trimming sets causes trimmed K-means and related variants to miss or poorly recover nearby or elongated clusters.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Theoretical work demonstrates that optimal trimming functions for alpha-trimmed K-means essentially coincide with indicator functions of unions of k balls of equal radius, which restricts effectiveness to spherical, well-separated clusters.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How to formulate computationally efficient, non-exhaustive optimal trimming algorithms that accommodate heterogeneous, non-spherical cluster geometries and unequal dispersion radii without incurring prohibitive combinatorial complexity.

related_papers.explanation: P003 extends spherical trimmed K-means using scatter estimation matrices (covariances) to handle elliptical distributions, but still relies on elliptical dispersion assumptions.

evidence.evidence: Note that, from Corollary 3.2, it follows that relatively nearby clusters could be badly detected if they are nonspherical or even if their shapes are too different because, according to that corollary, every cluster obtained with our method is spherical and all of them have the same radius.

research_gaps.gap: Absence of principled, automated approaches for estimating data-dependent trimming parameters (alpha) and minimum membership thresholds (s) in relaxed robust clustering frameworks.
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Practitioners are currently forced to test parameters over an arbitrary range or rely on manual tuning, limiting the deployment of robust trimmed K-means variants in automated, large-scale pipelines.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Relaxed continuous simplex formulations and trimmed K-means models successfully identify outliers and multi-membership clusters when trimming proportions alpha and minimum cluster memberships s are specified.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How to design fully automated, mathematically principled parameter selection mechanisms that estimate alpha and s dynamically during optimization.

related_papers.explanation: P009 highlights that currently there is no principled approach to estimating alpha and s, leaving it for future work.

evidence.evidence: At the moment, there is no principled approach to estimating the other two parameters alpha and s. We leave the investigation of such an approach for future work and demonstrate that RTKM remains competitive with existing methods over a range of alpha values.

research_gaps.gap: The mismatch between worst-case universal breakdown point vulnerability (O(1/n)) and robust practical performance under well-structured data assumptions.
research_gaps.why_it_matters: Worst-case theoretical analyses dictate that robust K-means and trimmed K-means can break down under arbitrary contamination with as few as one or two outliers, creating a false impression of fragility that contradicts their strong empirical success.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Universal breakdown point analyses prove that both biased and unbiased robust K-means objectives can fail under unrestricted contamination, whereas restricted analyses show they ignore outliers when inlier balls are sufficiently well-separated.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: Whether tighter non-asymptotic breakdown metrics can be established that bridge the gap between adversarial worst-case vulnerability and observed empirical robustness without requiring strict separation assumptions.

research_gaps.gap: Unresolved exponential dependence on the outlier count m in FPT approximation algorithms for metric clustering with outliers.
research_gaps.why_it_matters: State-of-the-art parameterized approximation algorithms for K-median and K-means with outliers exhibit polynomial-in-n running times with an exponential dependence ((k+m)/epsilon)^{O(m)} on the number of outliers m, limiting scalability when large contamination portions must be handled.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Approximation-preserving reductions using coreset constructions and ring partitioning can achieve optimal constant factor approximations in FPT time for metric clustering with outliers.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: Whether the exponential dependence on m is theoretically inherent or if approximation guarantees matching outlier-free K-means can be achieved with running times FPT in k and epsilon alone.

related_papers.explanation: P013 establishes the current FPT approximation framework and explicitly poses the open question of whether FPT dependence on m can be eliminated.

evidence.evidence: More fundamentally, perhaps, is the question whether we need an FPT dependence on the number of outliers, m; or whether it is possible to obtain approximation guarantees for k-MEDIANOUT matching that for k-MEDIAN, with a running time that is FPT in k and epsilon alone.

research_gaps.gap: Computational trade-offs and scalability bottlenecks of recursive, attribute-wise robust statistical rules (such as Tukey's fence or median absolute deviation) when applied to large-scale high-dimensional data streams.
research_gaps.why_it_matters: While attribute-wise robust outlier removal and adaptive boundaries improve clustering convergence and accuracy, computing them iteratively across high-dimensional features introduces significant computational overhead, precluding real-time and big-data applications.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Modified K-means algorithms using attribute-wise Tukey's rules or distance thresholds successfully isolate outliers and improve cluster purity on small- to medium-scale multivariate datasets.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How to reduce the time complexity of attribute-wise robust outlier removal procedures to make them computationally feasible for streaming big data without sacrificing outlier detection accuracy.

related_papers.explanation: P010 highlights that improving the runtime of modified K-means for big data clustering by reducing the time complexity of Tukey's rule is an open problem for future work.

evidence.evidence: Moreover, improving the run-time of modified K-means for big data clustering will be investigated further in future work by reducing the time complexity of Tukey's rule for outlier removal.

research_gaps.gap: Lack of streaming concept drift and adaptive refresh mechanisms for benign anchors in federated and distributed outlier-detection K-means deployments.
research_gaps.why_it_matters: IoT and networked systems experience continuous environmental changes and concept drift. Fixed, one-time commissioning anchors become stale over extended operational periods, degrading false-positive guarantees.
research_gaps.what_is_known: Adaptive federated baseline K-means achieves stable precision and low false-positive rates using static trusted benign anchors and robust worker-mean blending.
research_gaps.what_remains_unknown: How to design lightweight, streaming drift detectors and dynamic anchor-refresh protocols that maintain calibration validity under non-IID and drifting operational distributions.

related_papers.explanation: P017 identifies streaming concept drift and adaptive anchor refresh policies as the most immediate extensions needed for its federated framework.

evidence.evidence: The most immediate extension is streaming concept drift, using lightweight drift detectors or adaptive anchor refresh policies so that benign calibration remains valid over time...

hypotheses.hypothesis: Formulating optimal trimming regions as non-spherical geometric unions of dispersion-parameterized scatter matrices rather than equal-radius balls enables robust recovery of heterogeneous, nearby, or elongated clusters.
hypotheses.rationale: Standard trimmed K-means theoretical characterizations restrict optimal trimming sets and cluster boundaries to unions of spherical balls with equal radii, causing the algorithm to fail or badly detect nonspherical or differentially dispersed clusters.
hypotheses.testable_prediction: On synthetic and real datasets with elongated or heterogeneous elliptical dispersions, an elliptical-dispersion-based trimming formulation will achieve higher adjusted Rand index (ARI) and better cluster recovery compared to spherical trimmed K-means.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Evaluate spherical trimmed K-means and the proposed scatter-matrix-adjusted trimmed K-means variant across a suite of synthetic mixtures of elliptical and linear distributions with varying dispersion ratios, measuring cluster recovery and anomaly detection precision.

evidence.evidence: Note that, from Corollary 3.2, it follows that relatively nearby clusters could be badly detected if they are nonspherical or even if their shapes are too different because, according to that corollary, every cluster obtained with our method is spherical and all of them have the same radius.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Coupling relaxed continuous simplex clustering objectives with adaptive, objective-driven model selection criteria (such as adapted X-means/G-means splitting rules) enables automated, data-driven estimation of trimming proportions (alpha) and minimum memberships (s).
hypotheses.rationale: Current relaxed robust clustering frameworks rely on manual tuning or arbitrary parameter sweeps over alpha and s, limiting their deployment in fully automated, large-scale data pipelines.
hypotheses.testable_prediction: An automated parameter selection pipeline that optimizes RTKM objective bounds during iterative cluster splitting will estimate alpha and s within 5% of empirically optimal grid-search values while matching F1-score performance.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Benchmark the automated RTKM variant against grid-search-tuned RTKM across multiple multi-membership and single-membership outlier-contaminated datasets, recording execution time, F1-score, and deviation of estimated parameters from ground truth.

evidence.evidence: At the moment, there is no principled approach to estimating the other two parameters alpha and s. We leave the investigation of such an approach for future work and demonstrate that RTKM remains competitive with existing methods over a range of alpha values.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Establishing restricted non-asymptotic breakdown metrics under (rho_1, rho_2)-balanced inlier separation bounds eliminates the worst-case O(1/n) vulnerability paradox for robust K-means algorithms.
hypotheses.rationale: Universal breakdown point analyses dictate that robust K-means objectives fail under arbitrary contamination with as few as one or two outliers, creating a false impression of fragility that contradicts their strong empirical success on well-structured data.
hypotheses.testable_prediction: Under bounded well-separated inlier ball conditions, the maximum tolerable contamination fraction before cluster center perturbation exceeds delta scales independently of total sample size n for unbiased proximal maps.
hypotheses.proposed_test: Empirically measure the exact empirical breakdown point of robust K-means with unbiased proximal maps across synthetic datasets with systematically varied inter-cluster separation distances $v$ and increasing adversarial contamination proportions.

analysis.paper_title: Some Methods for Classification and Analysis of Multivariate Observations
analysis.research_question: How can we partition an N-dimensional population into k sets on the basis of a sample to achieve low within-class variance, what is the asymptotic behavior of such partitioning processes, and how can they be applied to practical multivariate analysis problems?
analysis.context: The paper addresses the problem of partitioning an N-dimensional population into k sets on the basis of a sample, originating from optimal information structure and classification problems. It proposes the k-means process as a computationally economical method to achieve partitions with low within-class variance, studies its asymptotic behavior using martingale theory, and extends the concepts to general metric spaces and practical applications like clustering, regression, and independence testing.
methods: k-means partitioning procedure for random sequences of points where each new point is assigned to the nearest mean and the group mean is updated sequentially
Coarsening and refining parameter modifications (parameters C and R) in computer implementations to control the number of groups k
Martingale theory and associated technical lemmas (such as bounding via Doob's martingale convergence theorem) to establish asymptotic properties and almost sure convergence
Fitting mixture of normal distributions to groups generated by minimum distance partitions for predictive regression and nonlinear discriminant analysis
Scrambled dimension test for independence among variables by comparing within-class variances before and after random association of marginal values
Distance-based classification trees for hierarchical lexigraphic filing and index systems
Two-step improvement procedure iterating between computing group means and reclassifying points based on nearness to these means
main_findings: The k-means sequence of random variables W(x^n) converges almost surely to V(x) for some x in the class of unbiased k-points (Theorem 1)
A strong law-like Cesàro average result establishes that the average distance between sample k-means and their conditional means goes to zero almost surely as m -> infinity (Theorem 2)

Computer implementations using coarsening (C) and refinement (R) parameters successfully group real-world multivariate data across various dimensions and sample sizes while maintaining stability across random processing orders
The k-means procedure combined with mixture-of-normals fitting yields effective nonlinear regression predictions and discriminant analysis performance
The k-means concept and its core analytical properties can be extended from Euclidean space to general compact metric spaces using sample centroids
assumptions: The probability measure p is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on E_N
p(R) = 1 for a closed and bounded convex set R subset of E_N, and p(A) > 0 for every open set A subset of R
Data points are selected independently using the fixed probability measure p
limitations_explicit: In general, the k-means procedure will not converge to an optimal partition that globally minimizes within-class variance, although there are special cases where it will
The paper lacks a fully satisfactory strong law of large numbers for k-means, relying instead on a weaker Cesàro-type convergence result (Theorem 2)
Theorem 1 does not completely eliminate the possibility that means might oscillate slowly but indefinitely around the center in certain symmetrical configurations
The statistical power of the proposed scrambled dimension test for independence remains to be fully seen and tested via large-scale computer programs
The extension of k-means to general metric spaces depends on whether the necessary computations for generalized centroids can be successfully accomplished

potential_open_questions.question: Can the k-means convergence guarantees be strengthened to eliminate the theoretical possibility of slow indefinite oscillation around central configurations?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The mathematical framework establishes almost sure convergence of the variance sequence and Cesàro averages, but certain symmetrical configurations leave open the behavior of the means themselves.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Theorem 1 establishes almost sure convergence but leaves open whether means oscillate.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: The k-means thus converge to some such relative position, but theorem 1 does not quite permit us to eliminate the interesting possibility that the two means oscillate slowly but indefinitely around the center. Theorem 1 provides for a.s. convergence of \sum_{i=1}^k p_i |x_i^n - u_i^n| to zero in a slightly broader class of situations. This is where the unbiased k-points x = (x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_k) with x_i \neq x_j for i \neq j, are all stable in the sense that for each such x, W(y) \geq W(x) (and hence V(y) \geq V(x)) for all y in a neighborhood of x. In this case, each such x falls in one of finitely many equivalence classes such that W is constant on each class.

potential_open_questions.question: What is the exact statistical power and practical performance of the scrambled dimension test for independence across diverse multivariate distributions?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Due to the lack of available computer programs for scrambling large punched card samples at the time of the study, extensive empirical testing of the test's power was not completed.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Lack of computing resources prevented full evaluation of the scrambling test's power.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: A computer program was not available to do the scrambling, and its being inconvenient to set up large numbers of scrambled samples using punched cards, further testing of this method was not undertaken. It is estimated, however, that an efficient computer program would easily permit this test to be applied at, say, the .01 level, on large samples in many dimensions. The power of this procedure remains to be seen. On the encouraging side is the related conjecture, that for fixed marginal distributions, the within-class variance for the optimal partition as defined in section 1 is maximal when the joint distribution is actually the product of the marginals.
sections: 3.4. A scrambled dimension test for independence among several variables

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: For fixed marginal distributions, the within-class variance for the optimal partition is maximal when the joint distribution is equal to the product of its marginals.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Intuitive reasoning and observations regarding scrambled variables suggest that destroying relationships by random association (making variables independent while preserving marginals) tends to increase the within-class variance.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Conjecture regarding maximal within-class variance under independence.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: The power of this procedure remains to be seen. On the encouraging side is the related conjecture, that for fixed marginal distributions, the within-class variance for the optimal partition as defined in section 1 is maximal when the joint distribution is actually the product of the marginals. If this is true (and it seems likely that it is, at least for a large class of reasonable distributions), then we reason that since the k-means process tends to give a good partition, this difference will be preserved in the scrambled and unscrambled variances, particularly for large samples. Variation in the within-class variance due to the random order in which the points are processed, can be reduced by taking several random orders, and averaging their result.
sections: 3.4. A scrambled dimension test for independence among several variables

analysis.paper_title: TRIMMED $k$-MEANS: AN ATTEMPT TO ROBUSTIFY QUANTIZERS
analysis.authors_year: J. A. Cuesta-Albertos, A. Gordaliza and C. Matrán, 1997
analysis.research_question: How to robustify $k$-means clustering through 'impartial trimming' (self-determined by the data), establish the mathematical existence and strong consistency of trimmed $k$-means, and analyze optimal trimming regions and practical computational performance.
analysis.context: Quantization of random variables and $k$-means clustering based on minimizing expected penalty functions suffer from instability and lack of robustness against outliers (e.g., standard joint location M-estimators or unrobust quantizers fail when extreme values are introduced). While trimming is a standard robust technique, traditional trimming suffers from arbitrariness in selecting removal zones. This paper extends Gordaliza's impartial trimming methodology to $k$-means to robustify clustering while avoiding arbitrary zone selection.
methods: Formulation of $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-means using trimming functions $\tau \in \tau_\alpha$ that generalize indicator functions of sets to allow partial participation and avoid arbitrary direction selection.
Mathematical analysis of optimal trimming regions, proving that best trimming functions essentially coincide with indicator functions of unions of $k$ balls of equal radius (Corollary 3.2).
Proof of existence of trimmed $k$-means (Theorem 3.1) and derivation of strong consistency properties via continuity results and the Skorohod representation theorem (Theorem 3.4, Theorem 3.6).

Simulation study using a simulated annealing based algorithm in Matlab on bivariate normal mixtures contaminated by outliers and inlayers to evaluate cluster recovery, anomaly detection, and mean estimation performance.
main_findings: The best trimming function for the $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-mean essentially coincides with the indicator function of a nonpathological set: the union of $k$ balls with the same radius (Corollary 3.2).
Trimmed $k$-means induce a partition of the optimal ball into $k$ clusters where each cluster center is a $\phi$-mean of the corresponding cluster (Proposition 3.3).

Under general conditions including the continuity of the limit probability distribution and uniqueness of the trimmed $k$-mean, empirical trimmed $k$-means are strongly consistent, converging in Hausdorff distance and in variation (Theorem 3.4, Theorem 3.6).

Simulations demonstrate that simulated annealing successfully computes trimmed $k$-means in practice, effectively detecting anomalies and estimating cluster means under high contamination, though low trimming levels can introduce estimator bias due to proximity between clusters.
assumptions: The penalty function $\phi: \mathbb{R}^+\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^+$ is continuous, nondecreasing, with $\phi(0)=0$ and $\phi(x)\to \infty$ as $x\to \infty$.
The underlying random vector $X$ has a probability distribution $P_X$ that is continuous (or absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure for specific boundary properties).
The true number of clusters $k$ is known and specified in advance.
limitations_explicit: There is an absence of a deterministic optimal (nonexhaustive) algorithm to choose the optimal trimming set.
Every cluster obtained with the method is spherical and all clusters share the same radius, meaning nearby nonspherical or differently shaped clusters may be poorly detected.

The breakdown point of the $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-means depends heavily on the data and can be low if the underlying proportion of anomalous points in a given cluster setup is large relative to $\alpha$.

potential_open_questions.question: How can trimmed $k$-means be extended or modified when clusters have non-spherical shapes or unequal dispersion radii?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The theoretical characterization shows optimal trimming sets and clusters are restricted to unions of balls of equal radius, making it difficult to properly model nonspherical or heterogeneous cluster dispersions.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Section 4, Page 9
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt:
Note that, from Corollary 3.2, it follows that relatively nearby clusters could be badly detected if they are nonspherical or even if their shapes are too different because, according to that corollary, every cluster obtained with our method is spherical and all of them have the same radius. Therefore, the ideal model would be one consisting of spherical, not too close, clusters. Moreover, in that ideal model, the anomalous observations should appear clearly separated from the nonanomalous ones.

Here we have chosen a sample of situations in which each requirement to have an ideal model is violated. Moreover, all of them have in common that many of the anomalous data are not so anomalous because the only restriction we have imposed on them is that they are not allowed to be in the 75% level confidence ellipsoids of the distributions generating the points in the clusters.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: The breakdown point of the $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-mean for a probability distribution supported by $k$ distinct clusters is bounded above by the minimum cluster probability proportion independent of the penalty function.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Examples with uniform distributions on discrete sets containing contamination show that if data naturally contains extraneous points or overlapping structures within the specified number of clusters, trimming cannot prevent contamination from shifting cluster centers arbitrarily if proportion thresholds are breached.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Section 5, Page 16
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt:
A careful look at this example shows that the cause of this behavior of the 2-mean procedure when applied to the uniform probability on A is that, if we are looking for just two clusters, then the set A already contains 1/3 of anomalous points (independently of when those points constitute or do not constitute a new cluster). Therefore, it seems that for probabilities Q, supported by a set which is divided into exactly k clusters with respective probabilities q1, q2, ..., qk, the breakdown point of the $\alpha$-trimmed $k$-mean of Q is, at most, $\inf\{\alpha, q_1, ..., q_k\}$ independently of $\Phi$. Of course, this fact is more apparent when we use other methods like the "two joint medians" example in the Introduction, which is clearly unstable in every circumstance.

In other words, the breakdown point generally depends, of course, on the procedure, but it also depends heavily on the data, in the sense that the same procedure can be highly stable with reasonable clusterized data when considering the right number of clusters, but it can also be very unstable in other cases. This is in some way natural and clearly related to the traditional key problem in cluster analysis: how to choose the number of clusters to look for?
